Casi veinte años antes de Lorenz, <stron: Almost twenty years before Lorenz, Mary Cartwright had already seen chaos, though without giving it that name. During the Second World War, the British government asked mathematicians for help with some radar amplifiers that were behaving erratically. Cartwright and John Littlewood studied the equation describing them, and proved that it had solutions of extraordinarily irregular behaviour, very sensitive to the conditions. The physicist Freeman Dyson, who attended one of her lectures, admitted decades later that he had failed to see the importance of what she was saying. In 1947 she became the first woman mathematician elected a Fellow of the Royal Society.

El caos es la razón por la que el tiempo: Chaos is the reason the weather cannot be predicted more than two weeks ahead, and not for want of computers. Lorenz discovered it in 1961 on re-entering a datum with three decimal places instead of six: the simulation separated completely from the earlier one. Since the atmosphere is never known with infinite precision, the error grows until it is the size of the prediction. That is why forecasts speak of probabilities and not of certainties, and why dozens of simulations are run with slightly different data.

El tema anterior clasificaba equilibrios: The previous topic classified equilibria: stable, unstable, centres. This topic shows what happens when a system falls into none of them. All you need is to know how to iterate a formula, as in [[fn-sucesiones|recurrence sequences]], and to remember the parabola. With that you see chaos being born, and with a logarithm you measure the dimension of a fractal.
En 1961 Edward Lorenz simulaba el clima: In 1961 Edward Lorenz was simulating the weather with a model of twelve equations. To repeat a simulation he typed the intermediate data in again, but rounded: 0.506 instead of 0.506127. He expected an insignificant difference. After two simulated months, the prediction bore no resemblance to the earlier one. That is where the expression butterfly effect was born, from the title of his 1972 lecture: “Does the flap of a butterfly's wings in Brazil set off a tornado in Texas?”. Poincaré had already sensed it in 1890 studying the three-body problem, but without computers nobody could see what it meant.
Entre $r = 3$ y $r \\approx 3{,}57$ la p: Between $r = 3$ and $r \approx 3{.}57$ the population goes from 2 to 4 to 8 values. Will each doubling take the same amount of $r$ as the previous one, or less and less?
Es una parábola. Nada más inofensivo. Y: It is a parabola. Nothing could be more harmless. And yet:
Esa autosemejanza —que un trozo ampliado: That self-similarity —a magnified piece resembling the whole— is what defines a fractal. And it forces us to rethink what dimension is. If you scale a figure by a factor $k$, its “size” is multiplied by $k^D$, where $D$ is the dimension: a line of doubled size is 2 times bigger ($2^1$), a square 4 times ($2^2$), a cube 8 ($2^3$). Rearranging:
This is the property that defines chaos. Two initial populations differing by one millionth follow identical paths... for a while. And then they separate completely.
Esto explica por qué el tiempo meteoroló: This explains why the weather cannot be predicted more than a few days ahead, however many satellites we put up. It is not ignorance: it is that the error grows exponentially. The climate (the long-term averages) is predictable; the weather on a particular Tuesday a month from now is not.
Fractal = autosemejanza. Su dimensión $D: Fractal = self-similarity. Its dimension $D = \log N/\log k$ need not be a whole number.
Fíjate en que hacer la diferencia inicia: Notice that making the initial difference a thousand times smaller does not delay the separation by a thousand years: only by a few. That is why measuring better does not solve the problem.
Hasta aquí, casi todo lo que has visto e: Up to here, almost everything you have seen was predictable: given the rules and the starting point, the result comes out. This topic is about the opposite discovery, and it is one of the most important of the twentieth century: there are completely deterministic systems —with no randomness at all— whose long-term behaviour is impossible to predict.
La dimensión fraccionaria no es una exce: Fractional dimension is no eccentricity: it measures roughness, and it is used in medicine. The branching of the vessels of a retina, that of the bronchial tree or the texture of a tissue have characteristic fractal dimensions, and departing from them is a sign of disease. In engineering, the fractal dimension of a surface predicts how it will wear or how much light it will reflect, and fractal aerials exploit repetition at different scales to work at many frequencies in very little space.
